claim: Transposable elements far surpass protein-coding genes in number in mammalian genomes, with approximately 25,000 protein-coding genes.
source: Millions of transposable elements reside in mammalian genomes, far surpassing in number the approximately 25000 protein-coding genes (Lander et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lander et al., 2001, which provides published evidence for this statement.

claim: Most transposable elements in mammalian genomes are retrotransposons that utilize an RNA intermediate to duplicate and mobilize.
source: Most of these elements are retrotransposons, which utilize an RNA intermediate to duplicate and mobilize.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retrotransposon biology.

claim: Transposons can modify gene functions through insertional mutagenesis, influence gene transcriptional outputs by acting as promoters or enhancers, or induce chromosomal rearrangements through non-allelic recombination.
source: They can modify gene functions through insertional mutagenesis, influence gene transcriptional outputs by acting as promoters or enhancers or induce chromosomal rearrangements through non-allelic recombination (Goodier and Kazazian, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goodier and Kazazian, 2008.

claim: Erratic transposon-related events have been linked to congenital diseases, cancer and infertility.
source: Accordingly, erratic transposon-related events have been linked to congenital diseases, cancer and infertility (Kaer and Speek, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaer and Speek, 2013.

claim: Transposons occupy approximately half of the genomic space in mammalian genomes.
source: Successive waves of transposon expansion and decline have shaped mammalian genomes over evolution, leading to a current occupancy rate of approximately half of the genomic space.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about transposon genomic occupancy.

claim: Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) comprise 12% of the mouse genome.
source: Long Terminal Repeat (LTR) sequences characterize endogenous retroviruses (ERVs, 12% of the mouse genome), which can be further subdivided into three families (ERV1, ERVK and ERVL), according to the infectious retroviruses they derive from (Stocking and Kozak, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stocking and Kozak, 2008.

claim: LINEs comprise 20% of the mouse genome and SINEs comprise 8%.
source: Non-LTR elements comprise Long and Short INterspersed Elements (LINEs and SINEs, 20% and 8% of the genome, respectively), and also consist of specific sub-families (Babushok et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Babushok et al., 2007.

claim: Around 1-2% of LINEs and ERVs have intact sequences that embed the protein coding information necessary for their mobilization.
source: The majority of transposons have accumulated nullifying mutations and truncations, but around 1–2% of LINEs and ERVs have intact sequences that embed the protein coding information necessary for their mobilization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about transposon integrity.

claim: ERVK elements cause at least 10% of spontaneous mutations in laboratory mice.
source: Notably, ERVK elements show the greatest level of activity, which causes at least 10% of spontaneous mutations in laboratory mice (Maksakova et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maksakova et al., 2006.

claim: In somatic cells and in the male differentiating germline, DNA methylation is the main transcriptional suppressor of LTR and non-LTR transposons.
source: In somatic cells and in the male differentiating germline, DNA methylation is the main transcriptional suppressor of LTR and non-LTR transposons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about transposon control mechanisms.

claim: Transposable elements are densely methylated in somatic cells and in the male differentiating germline.
source: In these contexts, transposable elements are densely methylated (Rollins et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2012) and DNA hypomethylation leads to their de-repression (Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Walsh et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rollins et al., 2006 and Smith et al., 2012.

claim: DNA hypomethylation leads to transposon de-repression in somatic cells and in the male differentiating germline.
source: In these contexts, transposable elements are densely methylated (Rollins et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2012) and DNA hypomethylation leads to their de-repression (Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004; Walsh et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bourc'his and Bestor, 2004 and Walsh et al., 1998.

claim: The early germline and the early embryo manage to globally control their transposon burden without DNA methylation.
source: In contrast, the early germline and the early embryo manage to globally control their transposon burden without DNA methylation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about transposon control in early development.

claim: The early germline and early embryo naturally undergo genome-wide loss of DNA methylation, likely as part of the acquisition of a pluripotent, flexible state.
source: These cells naturally undergo genome-wide loss of DNA methylation, likely as part of the acquisition of a pluripotent, flexible state (Seisenberger et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seisenberger et al., 2013, with speculative reasoning about the purpose.

claim: Mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells can use DNA methylation-independent mechanisms to silence transposons.
source: Moreover, genetic studies have demonstrated that mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells can use DNA methylation-independent mechanisms to silence transposons: knocking-out the three active DNA methyltransferases (Dnmt-tKO) does not yield significant de-repression of transposons, except Intracisternal A Particle (IAP) elements (Karimi et al., 2011b; Matsui et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karimi et al., 2011b and Matsui et al., 2010.

claim: Knocking-out the three active DNA methyltransferases (Dnmt-tKO) in mouse ES cells does not yield significant de-repression of transposons, except Intracisternal A Particle (IAP) elements.
source: Moreover, genetic studies have demonstrated that mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells can use DNA methylation-independent mechanisms to silence transposons: knocking-out the three active DNA methyltransferases (Dnmt-tKO) does not yield significant de-repression of transposons, except Intracisternal A Particle (IAP) elements (Karimi et al., 2011b; Matsui et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karimi et al., 2011b and Matsui et al., 2010.

claim: H3K9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) is deposited by the EHMT2/G9a and EHMT1/GLP lysine methyltransferases.
source: H3K9 dimethylation (H3K9me2), which is deposited by the EHMT2/G9a and EHMT1/GLP lysine methyltransferases, directly and specifically represses class L ERVs (Maksakova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maksakova et al., 2013.

claim: H3K9me2 directly and specifically represses class L ERVs.
source: H3K9 dimethylation (H3K9me2), which is deposited by the EHMT2/G9a and EHMT1/GLP lysine methyltransferases, directly and specifically represses class L ERVs (Maksakova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maksakova et al., 2013.

claim: H3K9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) can be catalyzed by the SETDB1 (also known as ESET) or the SUV39H enzymes.
source: H3K9 trimethylation (H3K9me3) can be catalyzed by the SETDB1 (also known as ESET) or the SUV39H enzymes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about H3K9me3 enzymes.

claim: The SUV39H system targets H3K9me3 at evolutionarily young LTR and non-LTR transposons.
source: The SUV39H system targets H3K9me3 at evolutionary young LTR and non-LTR transposons, but Suv39h mutant ES cells principally up-regulate LINE1 elements (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014.

claim: Suv39h mutant ES cells principally up-regulate LINE1 elements.
source: The SUV39H system targets H3K9me3 at evolutionary young LTR and non-LTR transposons, but Suv39h mutant ES cells principally up-regulate LINE1 elements (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014.

claim: SETDB1, together with its associated co-repressor TRIM28 (also known as KAP1), mainly control H3K9me3-dependent suppression of ERVK transposons.
source: In parallel, SETDB1, together with its associated co-repressor, the Krüppel-associated box domain (KRAB)-Associated Protein 1 (TRIM28, also known as KAP1), mainly control H3K9me3-dependent suppression of ERVK transposons- a family to which IAP elements belong (Karimi et al., 2011b; Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karimi et al., 2011b, Matsui et al., 2010, and Rowe et al., 2010.

claim: IAP elements belong to the ERVK transposon family.
source: In parallel, SETDB1, together with its associated co-repressor, the Krüppel-associated box domain (KRAB)-Associated Protein 1 (TRIM28, also known as KAP1), mainly control H3K9me3-dependent suppression of ERVK transposons- a family to which IAP elements belong (Karimi et al., 2011b; Matsui et al., 2010; Rowe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about IAP classification.

claim: TRIM28 is recruited to specific genomic sites via direct interactions with KRAB-zinc finger proteins.
source: TRIM28 is recruited to specific genomic sites via direct interactions with KRAB-zinc finger proteins (Friedman et al., 1996), which are a large family of DNA binding factors that co-evolved with ERVs (Emerson and Thomas, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Friedman et al., 1996.

claim: KRAB-zinc finger proteins are a large family of DNA binding factors that co-evolved with ERVs.
source: TRIM28 is recruited to specific genomic sites via direct interactions with KRAB-zinc finger proteins (Friedman et al., 1996), which are a large family of DNA binding factors that co-evolved with ERVs (Emerson and Thomas, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Emerson and Thomas, 2009.

claim: Only Murine Leukemia Virus (MuLV) elements are reactivated upon H3K27me3 deficiency in ES cells.
source: In contrast, the repressive spectrum of polycomb-mediated H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) is limited: only Murine Leukemia Virus (MuLV) elements are reactivated upon H3K27me3 deficiency (Leeb et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leeb et al., 2010.

claim: ES cells grown in standard serum-based conditions have heavily methylated genomes (~75% of CpG methylation).
source: ES cells grown in standard serum-based conditions have heavily methylated genomes (~75% of CpG methylation)(Stadler et al., 2011), which is linked to the expression of de novo DNA methyltransferases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stadler et al., 2011.

claim: ES cells grown in presence of two small kinase inhibitors (2i) down-regulate de novo DNA methyltransferases and have reduced DNA methylation levels.
source: ES cells grown in presence of two small kinase inhibitors (2i) down-regulate these enzymes, and have reduced DNA methylation levels (Leitch et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leitch et al., 2013 and Ying et al., 2008.

claim: Upon transfer from serum to 2i medium, demethylation occurs with a slow kinetics, requiring several weeks to reach 20-30% of CpG methylation.
source: Upon transfer from serum to 2i medium, demethylation occurs with a slow kinetics: several weeks are required to reach 20–30% of CpG methylation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about 2i-induced demethylation kinetics.

claim: Imprinted genes, major satellite repeats and IAP elements maintain persistent DNA methylation after 2i adaptation.
source: Notably, imprinted genes, major satellite repeats and IAP elements maintain persistent DNA methylation after 2i adaptation (Ficz et al., 2013; Habibi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ficz et al., 2013 and Habibi et al., 2013.

claim: Addition of vitamin C (vitC) can lower the ES cell methylome by promoting active demethylation through stimulating the TET (Ten Eleven Translocation) enzymes.
source: Addition of vitamin C (vitC) can also lower the ES cell methylome. This compound promotes active demethylation by stimulating the TET (Ten Eleven Translocation) enzymes, which oxidize 5-methylcytosines to 5-hydroxymethylcytosines that are potential intermediates towards unmethylated cytosines (Blaschke et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blaschke et al., 2013.

claim: TET enzymes oxidize 5-methylcytosines to 5-hydroxymethylcytosines that are potential intermediates towards unmethylated cytosines.
source: This compound promotes active demethylation by stimulating the TET (Ten Eleven Translocation) enzymes, which oxidize 5-methylcytosines to 5-hydroxymethylcytosines that are potential intermediates towards unmethylated cytosines (Blaschke et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blaschke et al., 2013.

claim: CpG methylation linearly decreased from 77% to 13% in six days during serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: Quantification using the methyl-CpG sensitive restriction enzyme-based LUminometric Methylation Assay (LUMA) (Karimi et al., 2011a) revealed that CpG methylation linearly decreased from 77% to 13% in six days, and reached a minimal level of 6% after 14 days of conversion (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A using the LUMA assay.

claim: CpG methylation reached a minimal level of 6% after 14 days of serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: Quantification using the methyl-CpG sensitive restriction enzyme-based LUminometric Methylation Assay (LUMA) (Karimi et al., 2011a) revealed that CpG methylation linearly decreased from 77% to 13% in six days, and reached a minimal level of 6% after 14 days of conversion (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A using the LUMA assay.

claim: Cells grown in serum+vitC or in 2i-only maintained relatively high CpG methylation content after the same treatment duration, with an average of 56% and 22%, respectively.
source: In comparison, cells grown in serum+vitC or in 2i-only maintained relatively high CpG methylation content after the same treatment duration, with an average of 56% and 22%, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), in agreement with a previous study (Habibi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Habibi et al., 2013.

claim: Rapid and extensive loss of genomic methylation can only be attained through the synergistic action of 2i-dependent passive demethylation and vitC-dependent active demethylation.
source: This suggests that such a rapid and extensive loss of genomic methylation can only be attained through the synergistic action of 2i-dependent passive demethylation and vitC-dependent active demethylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different culture conditions.

claim: Young LINE1 transposons (L1-A and L1-T) mirrored the dynamics of the genome average during demethylation.
source: All analyzed sequences reached very low levels of CpG methylation upon 2+vitC switch, although at various rates. Young LINE1 transposons (L1-A and L1-T) mirrored the dynamics of the genome average, while the CpG-rich promoter of the germline-specific gene Dazl was a fast 'loser', comparatively.
evidence: This is based on bisulfite-pyrosequencing data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The demethylation rate of IAP transposons and the Imprinting Control Region (ICR) of the H19-Igf2 locus was slower than the rest of genome.
source: Consistent with their intrinsic ability to maintain high levels of DNA methylation in various contexts of global DNA hypomethylation (Ficz et al., 2013; Seisenberger et al., 2013), the demethylation rate of IAP transposons and the Imprinting Control Region (ICR) of the H19-Igf2 locus was slower than the rest of genome.
evidence: This is based on bisulfite-pyrosequencing data and supported by citations to Ficz et al., 2013 and Seisenberger et al., 2013.

claim: The combination of 2i and vitC eventually overcame chromatin environments that confer protection of IAP and H19-Igf2 ICR sequences from DNA demethylation.
source: Nevertheless, the combination of 2i and vitC eventually overcame chromatin environments that confer protection of these sequences from DNA demethylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the bisulfite-pyrosequencing data showing eventual demethylation.

claim: ES cells grown in 2i+vitC were almost completely unmethylated, with an average CpG methylation of 4.6%.
source: Available methylome maps indicate that 71% and 30% of CpG sites are methylated in serum and in 2i-only conditions, respectively (Habibi et al., 2013; Seisenberger et al., 2012; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1); in contrast, ES cells grown in 2i+vitC were almost completely unmethylated, with an average CpG methylation of 4.6%, which is fully consistent with the LUMA quantification (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with LUMA data.

claim: Low methylation levels were homogeneously found throughout all genomic compartments in 2i+vitC conditions, including single-copy genic regions and repeated sequences.
source: Low methylation levels were homogeneously found throughout all genomic compartments, including single-copy genic regions and repeated sequences (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All transposable element families (ERVs, LINEs and SINEs) were affected by 2i+vitC-induced demethylation.
source: In particular, all transposable element families (ERVs, LINEs and SINEs) were affected by 2i+vitC-induced demethylation (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 4,100 Residually Methylated Regions (RMRs) were identified in 2i+vitC conditions, which exhibited an average of 26% of CpG methylation after long-term conversion.
source: In an attempt to identify individual genomic regions with significant DNA methylation traces (Song et al., 2013), we uncovered 4,100 Residually Methylated Regions (RMRs) (Figure 1F,G), which exhibited an average of 26% of CpG methylation after long-term 2i+vitC conversion.
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data analysis shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Nearly 75% of the RMRs overlapped with repeated sequences, among which half belonged to the ERVK class.
source: We estimated that nearly 75% of the RMRs overlapped with repeated sequences, among which half belonged to the ERVK class.
evidence: This is based on analysis of WGBS data and RMR annotation.

claim: One quarter of the repeat-associated RMRs overlapped with LINEs, specifically localized around 5' UTR regions.
source: One quarter of the repeat-associated RMRs overlapped with LINEs, however specifically localized around 5' UTR regions; in contrast, ERVK-associated RMRs encompassed the entire length of these elements (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ERVK-associated RMRs encompassed the entire length of these elements.
source: One quarter of the repeat-associated RMRs overlapped with LINEs, however specifically localized around 5' UTR regions; in contrast, ERVK-associated RMRs encompassed the entire length of these elements (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Imprinting Control Regions (ICRs), which are usually protected against DNA methylation erasure in 2i conditions, were devoid of any residual DNA methylation in 2i+vitC.
source: Notably, Imprinting Control Regions (ICRs), which are usually protected against DNA methylation erasure in 2i conditions, were devoid of any residual DNA methylation in 2i+VitC (Figure 1—figure supplements 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGBS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1D,E.

claim: Global CpG methylation levels less than 5% are unprecedented in male WT cells, both in culture and in vivo.
source: Global CpG methylation levels, less than 5%, are unprecedented in male WT cells, both in culture and in vivo (Seisenberger et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seisenberger et al., 2013.

claim: LINE1, IAPEz and MERVL transposons undergo a two-phase pattern of regulation during serum to 2i+vitC conversion: initial up-regulation culminating at day 6, then re-silencing in the absence of DNA methylation.
source: Through a time-course RT-qPCR analysis of steady-state levels of three classes of retrotranscripts (LINE1, IAPEz and MERVL), we observed a two-phase pattern: 1) an initial up-regulation, which culminates at day 6 (D6) of 2i+vitC conversion, when genomic methylation reaches a low plateau, then 2) re-silencing in the absence of DNA methylation (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The biphasic pattern of transposon regulation was confirmed by amplification-free Nanostring nCounter quantification and extended to VL30 elements.
source: This was confirmed by amplification-free Nanostring nCounter quantification and further extended to VL30 elements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The same biphasic pattern of transposon regulation was reproduced in E14 ES cells exposed to 2i+vitC.
source: To rule out background-specific effects, we exposed serum-cultured E14 ES cells to 2i+vitC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). Despite some differences in the magnitude of transposon de-repression observed between the J1 and E14 cell lines, the same biphasic pattern of regulation was reproduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The quantity of transposon transcripts remained constant during the conversion from serum to 2i-only or from serum to serum+vitC.
source: By contrast, the quantity of transposon transcripts remained constant during the conversion from serum to 2i-only or from serum to serum+vitC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which further underscores the synergistic effect of 2i and vitC in releasing DNA methylation-based repression of transposons.
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The transposon transcription burst did not occur upon conversion of Dnmt-tKO cells.
source: Importantly, the transposon transcription burst did not occur upon conversion of Dnmt-tKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Rapid transition from a methylated to an unmethylated state provides a window for transposon reactivation.
source: Rapid transition from a methylated to an unmethylated state seems to provide a window for transposon reactivation; this is in agreement with the hypothesis that Dnmt-tKO ES cells have likely acquired long-term compensatory mechanisms preventing this relaxation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of WT and Dnmt-tKO cell behavior.

claim: Both LINE1-ORF1 and IAP-gag proteins presented a peak of expression at D6 during serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: We further found that the burst of transposon expression also occurs at the protein level: both LINE1-ORF1 and IAP-gag proteins presented a peak of expression at D6, which we detected by western blotting (Figure 2B) and by quantification of immunofluorescence signals (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B and immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: LINE1 protein intensity showed great inter-cellular variability, ranging from intense to no signal.
source: While IAP-gag staining was uniform among cells at a given time point, LINE1 protein intensity showed great inter-cellular variability, ranging from intense to no signal.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification data.

claim: The level of LINE1 heterogeneity was present throughout the conversion process from serum to 2i+vitC conditions, including at D6.
source: Importantly, the level of LINE1 heterogeneity was present throughout the conversion process from serum to 2i+vitC conditions, including at D6.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence quantification data.

claim: LINE1 heterogeneous expression is not linked to various degrees of pluripotency.
source: In an attempt to link this heterogeneity with fluctuating levels of pluripotency, we performed co-staining against NANOG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). We could not detect any correlations suggesting that LINE1 heterogeneous expression is not linked to various degrees of pluripotency.
evidence: This is based on co-immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cell proliferation remained globally constant over the 14-day period of media conversion.
source: We found cell proliferation to remain globally constant over the 14-day period of media conversion, as measured by division rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), transcriptional level of different proliferation markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) or percentage of histone H3 Serine 10 phosphorylation-positive cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, 3B, and 3C.

claim: Increased cell death/apoptosis was not observed at any days during the conversion.
source: Similarly, we did not observe increased cell death/apoptosis at any days during the conversion (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Despite the transient release of transposon silencing at D6, transposon multiplication or transposon-induced chromosome rearrangements were not detected.
source: Finally, despite the transient release of transposon silencing at D6, we failed to detect transposon multiplication or transposon-induced chromosome rearrangements: genomic copy numbers of LINE1 and IAPEz elements as well as karyotypes were globally similar between cells before (D0) and after the transposon burst (D14) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: 2i+vitC induces a transient up-regulation of transposon transcription and translation, but cellular viability and genome integrity remain largely intact.
source: In sum, 2i+vitC induces a transient up-regulation of transposon transcription and translation, but cellular viability and genome integrity remain largely intact.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: A total of 58 transposon families were found differentially expressed between at least two of the time points of medium conversion.
source: By allowing multiple hits and by weighting each read by its hit number, a total of 58 transposon families were found differentially expressed between at least two of the time points of medium conversion (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Almost all transposon families underwent significant up-regulation from D0 to D6.
source: Volcano plots show that almost all families underwent significant up-regulation from D0 to D6 (Figure 2D, left panel), ranging from modest (LINEs) to robust (MMERGLN) fold changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D, left panel.

claim: Silencing restoration occurred globally between D6 and D13, except for IAPEy or B1 elements, which remained at constant levels.
source: Silencing restoration also occurred globally between D6 and D13, except for IAPEy or B1 elements, which remained at constant levels (Figure 2D, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D, middle panel.

claim: Some transposon families, such as MERVL, SINEs B2 or any LINE1 types, were more strongly repressed after the 2i+vitC conversion at D13 than initially at D0 in serum.
source: Some families, such as MERVL, SINEs B2 or any LINE1 types, were more strongly repressed after the 2i+vitC conversion at D13 than initially at D0 in serum.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Other transposon families, like MMERGLN, ETnERV3 and IAPEz, underwent repression from D6 to D13, but not to the full extent when compared to D0.
source: Others, like MMERGLN, ETnERV3 and IAPEz, underwent repression from D6 to D13, but not to the full extent when compared to D0.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 7163 uniquely identifiable LINEs and 2372 ERVs showed activity throughout the conversion.
source: We found that 7163 uniquely identifiable LINEs and 2372 ERVs showed activity throughout the conversion, which represented 1.2% and 3.8% of the total number of LINE1s and ERVs, respectively, or 19.3% and 15.2% of the intact elements of these families (integrity score >0.8).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq unique mapping analysis.

claim: Within all transposon families, the number of significantly expressed elements was higher at D6 than at D0 or D13 of conversion.
source: Within all families, the number of significantly expressed elements was higher at D6 than at D0 or D13 of conversion (Supplementary file 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Supplementary file 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Not only were more transposon elements active at D6, but individual copies also gained expression at D6.
source: Generally, not only were more elements active, but individual copies also gained expression at D6 (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D,E.

claim: Active transposons were evenly distributed along chromosomes, with no particular genomic hotspot.
source: Finally, active transposons were evenly distributed along chromosomes, with no particular genomic hotspot (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4F.

claim: Expression levels were the most homogeneous among elements of the same family during the D6 de-repression phase.
source: Most importantly, it uncovered unprecedented details into the diverse regulation of individual transposons. Expression levels were the most homogeneous among elements of the same family during the D6 de-repression phase.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq unique mapping analysis.

claim: At the D13 silencing restoration time-point, heterogenic regulation was observed at the inter- and intra-familial levels.
source: Comparatively, at the D13 silencing restoration time-point, we observed heterogenic regulation at the inter- and intra-familial levels (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: LINEs and MMERGLN families displayed collective behaviors, with the vast majority of elements simultaneously undergoing repression at D13.
source: Some families, such as LINEs and MMERGLN, displayed collective behaviors, with the vast majority of elements simultaneously undergoing repression.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq unique mapping analysis.

claim: IAPEz, MERVL or ETn elements showed the widest distribution in individual expression at D13.
source: In contrast, IAPEz, MERVL or ETn elements showed the widest distribution in individual expression.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq unique mapping analysis.

claim: IAPEz elements were split into two categories at D13, one that maintained high expression, and the other that underwent complete silencing.
source: In particular, IAPEz elements were split into two categories at D13, one that maintained high expression, and the other that underwent complete silencing.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq unique mapping analysis.

claim: Compared to transposons, protein-coding genes followed different dynamics during 2i+vitC conversion.
source: Compared to transposons, protein-coding genes followed different dynamics during 2i+vitC conversion (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The vast majority of protein-coding genes exhibited stable expression during 2i+vitC conversion, while 3,301 genes were either up- or down-regulated.
source: The vast majority exhibited stable expression, while 3,301 genes were either up- or down-regulated; these numbers are similar to previous reports of a serum to 2i transcriptional switch (Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and a citation to Marks et al., 2012.

claim: Most differentially expressed genes displayed a monotonic pattern during 2i+vitC conversion.
source: While the general expression trend for transposons was biphasic, most differentially expressed genes displayed a monotonic pattern.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The Dazl gene was continuously up-regulated from D0 to D13, reflecting its sensitivity to vitC.
source: A relevant example is the Dazl gene, which was continuously up-regulated from D0 to D13 (Figure 3B), reflecting its sensitivity to vitC (Blaschke et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Blaschke et al., 2013.

claim: Expression of genes encoding transcription factors of the ZSCAN4 family progressively decreased during the conversion, with undetectable transcripts by D13.
source: Conversely, expression of genes encoding transcription factors of the ZSCAN4 family progressively decreased during the conversion, with undetectable transcripts by D13 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 2-cell-like cells exist in serum-based conditions but disappear in 2i+vitC medium.
source: As expression of these factors reflects a subpopulation of ES cells exhibiting a transcriptional profile akin to 2-cell stage embryos (Macfarlan et al., 2012), our results imply that 2-cell-like cells exist in serum-based conditions but disappear in 2i+vitC medium.
evidence: This is inferred from the ZSCAN4 expression data and a citation to Macfarlan et al., 2012.

claim: 156 genes adopted a transposon-type pattern, with a peak at D6 followed by subsequent down-regulation at D13.
source: The burst of expression at D6 appears specific to transposons, and is not a general trend of the genome. Nevertheless, 156 genes adopted a transposon-type pattern, with a peak at D6 followed by subsequent down-regulation at D13 (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Genes with transposon-type expression patterns were linked to ontology categories such as organismal development and were significantly enriched for transcription factors, most notably those related to pluripotency.
source: These genes were linked to ontology categories such as organismal development and were significantly enriched for transcription factors, most notably those related to pluripotency (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Transcription of Nanog, Klf4, Tbx3 and Prmd14 peaked at D6.
source: Further examination indicated that transcription of Nanog, Klf4, Tbx3 and Prmd14 peaked at D6 (Figure 3C); enhanced production of pluripotency-related proteins was also observed by western blot within the first few days of 2i+vitC conversion (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C and western blot data in Figure 3D.

claim: Enhanced production of pluripotency-related proteins was observed by western blot within the first few days of 2i+vitC conversion.
source: Further examination indicated that transcription of Nanog, Klf4, Tbx3 and Prmd14 peaked at D6 (Figure 3C); enhanced production of pluripotency-related proteins was also observed by western blot within the first few days of 2i+vitC conversion (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The peak of transposon transcription at D6 coincides with a maximum availability of pluripotency regulators.
source: Therefore, the peak of transposon transcription at D6 coincides with a maximum availability of pluripotency regulators.
evidence: This is inferred from the coincident timing of transposon and pluripotency factor expression peaks.

claim: LTR sequences of ERVs can direct transcription of nearby genes in ES cells and early embryos, forming chimeric transcripts.
source: It was previously shown that LTR sequences of ERVs can direct transcription of nearby genes in ES cells and early embryos, forming chimeric transcripts (Karimi et al., 2011b; Macfarlan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karimi et al., 2011b and Macfarlan et al., 2012.

claim: Several dozens of genes used a promoter located in a transposable element (ERV or LINE1), independently of the medium composition.
source: We detected several dozens of genes that used a promoter located in a transposable element (ERV or LINE1), independently of the medium composition (Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Mep1b gene was induced ten-fold at D6, concomitant with the activation of the RLTR9E element driving its expression, before returning to its initial level at D13.
source: A particular case was Mep1b, which clusters with the 156 'transposon-like' genes. This gene was induced ten-fold at D6, concomitant with the activation of the RLTR9E element driving its expression, before returning to its initial level at D13 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The genome-wide relaxation of transposons had generally a minimal effect on protein-coding gene expression.
source: Although the burst of transposon expression at D6 can sporadically coordinate the transient activation of adjacent genes, it can be concluded that the genome-wide relaxation of transposons had generally a minimal effect on protein-coding gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data analysis showing limited gene-transposon coordination.

claim: H3K9me3 marks remained globally constant during serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: By western blot and immunostaining, we observed large-scale reorganization of histone modifications linked to transcriptional repression. While H3K9me3 marks remained globally constant, H3K9me2 levels were strongly reduced and, inversely, H3K27me3 levels increased from the first days of conversion (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K9me2 levels were strongly reduced during serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: By western blot and immunostaining, we observed large-scale reorganization of histone modifications linked to transcriptional repression. While H3K9me3 marks remained globally constant, H3K9me2 levels were strongly reduced and, inversely, H3K27me3 levels increased from the first days of conversion (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K27me3 levels increased from the first days of serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: By western blot and immunostaining, we observed large-scale reorganization of histone modifications linked to transcriptional repression. While H3K9me3 marks remained globally constant, H3K9me2 levels were strongly reduced and, inversely, H3K27me3 levels increased from the first days of conversion (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The global dynamics of histone marks were not correlated with the changes in the availability of H3K9me2 modifiers and components of the polycomb machinery.
source: The global dynamics of histone marks were not correlated with the changes in the availability—or lack thereof—of H3K9me2 modifiers and components of the polycomb machinery (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: H3K9me2 was either constitutively absent or rapidly removed at several transposon types upon 2i+vitC conversion.
source: ChIP-qPCR measurement confirmed either the constitutive absence or the rapid removal of H3K9me2 at several transposon types upon 2i+vitC conversion (Figure 4B), making it unlikely that this mark could participate to long-term transposon silencing in the absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ehmt2-KO ES cells did not exhibit significant up-regulation of transposons when cultured in serum, with the exception of MERVL elements.
source: As previously described, when cultured in serum, Ehmt2-KO ES cells did not exhibit significant up-regulation of transposons as measured by Nanostring, with the exception of MERVL elements (Macfarlan et al., 2012; Maksakova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data and citations to Macfarlan et al., 2012 and Maksakova et al., 2013.

claim: Upon 2i+vitC conversion, while LINE1 elements behaved as in WT cells, IAPEz and MERVL expression was enhanced around D6 in Ehmt2-KO cells.
source: Upon 2i+vitC conversion, while LINE1 elements behaved as in WT cells, IAPEz and MERVL expression was enhanced around D6 in Ehmt2-KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ehmt2 mutants exhibited transposon re-silencing after D6, which excludes a role for H3K9me2 in compensating the loss of DNA methylation-dependent repression.
source: Most importantly, Ehmt2 mutants exhibited transposon re-silencing after D6, which excludes a role for H3K9me2 in compensating the loss of DNA methylation-dependent repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the Nanostring data in Ehmt2-KO cells.

claim: Neither the total number of H3K9me3 peaks nor their preferential occurrence on transposons was significantly altered during the serum to 2i+vitC conversion.
source: Neither the total number of H3K9me3 peaks (39424 at D0 and 38554 at D15), nor their preferential occurrence on transposons was significantly altered during the conversion (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of H3K27me3-enriched regions raised four fold from D0 to D15 (9663 to 40098).
source: In contrast, the number of H3K27me3-enriched regions raised four fold from D0 to D15 (9663 to 40098).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: The vast majority of newly gained H3K27me3 peaks were located in ERV and LINE1 repeats, at the expense of gene promoters.
source: The vast majority of newly gained H3K27me3 peaks were located in ERV and LINE1 repeats, at the expense of gene promoters (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A gradual H3K27me3 re-localization to pericentric heterochromatin was observed during the conversion.
source: We also observed a gradual H3K27me3 re-localization to pericentric heterochromatin during the conversion, by ChIP-qPCR at major satellite repeats (Figure 4D), by immunostaining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and by mapping ChIP-seq reads to the major satellite consensus sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 4D, immunostaining in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and ChIP-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Redistribution of H3K27me3 from gene promoters towards satellite repeats was previously reported in 2i-only conditions.
source: Redistribution of H3K27me3 from gene promoters towards satellite repeats was previously reported in 2i-only conditions (Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marks et al., 2012.

claim: Increased H3K27me3 levels and subsequent accumulation at different transposon repeats seems specific to the globally hypomethylated genome of 2i+vitC-cultured cells.
source: However, increased H3K27me3 levels and subsequent accumulation at different transposon repeats seems specific to the globally hypomethylated genome of 2i+vitC-cultured cells.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with 2i-only conditions.

claim: Hypomethylated Dnmt-tKO ES cells grown in serum displayed similar H3K27me3 redistribution towards transposons.
source: Accordingly, hypomethylated Dnmt-tKO ES cells grown in serum displayed similar H3K27me3 redistribution towards transposons when we analyzed available ChIP-seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The 5' UTR of LINEs (L1-A and L1-T) and the LTR of IAPEz were enriched in H3K4me3.
source: In agreement with the high expression of these elements, the 5' UTR of LINEs (L1-A and L1-T) and the LTR of IAPEz were enriched in H3K4me3, as assessed by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Active LINE1 elements (marked by H3K4me3) had lower DNA methylation levels compared to inactive ones (marked by H3K9me3).
source: Interestingly, bisulfite-pyrosequencing analysis of H3K4me3- or H3K9me3-immunoprecipitated chromatin confirmed, as expected, that active LINE1 elements (marked by H3K4me3) had lower DNA methylation levels compared to inactive ones (marked by H3K9me3)(Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-bisulfite-pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: At D0 in serum, most transposon families were occupied by H3K9me3 to various extents, but lacked H3K27me3.
source: At D0 in serum, most transposon families were occupied by H3K9me3 to various extents, but lacked H3K27me3 (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: RLTR4 exhibited a strong H3K27me3 signal at D0 in serum.
source: One noticeable exception was RLTR4, which exhibited a strong H3K27me3 signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: RLTR4 is 90% identical to MuLV.
source: Interestingly, this element is 90% identical to MuLV, which is one of the few transposons up-regulated in polycomb-deficient ES cells (Leeb et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation to Leeb et al., 2010.

claim: Upon 2i+vitC conversion, H3K9me3 levels remained largely constant, although patterns observed in serum tended to be exacerbated.
source: Upon 2i+vitC conversion, H3K9me3 levels remained largely constant, although patterns observed in serum tended to be exacerbated: families with the initial highest enrichment (IAPEz, RLTR6 and MMERVK10C) were further enriched for this mark, while families with modest enrichment (MERVL, MURVY or the MalR-class L ORR1A and ORR1B) tended to lose it.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: H3K27me3 progressively accumulated at most transposons upon 2i+vitC conversion, with variable gain among families.
source: Meanwhile, H3K27me3 progressively accumulated at most transposons (Figure 4E), and this gain was variable among families: from inexistent for IAPEz to moderate for LINEs and VL30, and to strong for various ERVs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: High levels of H3K9 or H3K27 methylation in ERV elements were found to be restricted to full-length intact elements; isolated solitary (solo) LTRs had most often no enrichment for H3K9 or H3K27 methylation.
source: Of note, when focusing on ERV elements, high levels of H3K9 or H3K27 methylation were found to be restricted to full-length intact elements: isolated solitary (solo) LTRs (not interspersed with other repeats) had most often no enrichment for H3K9 or H3K27 methylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Internal ERV sequences are important for H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 recruitment.
source: This suggests that internal ERV sequences are important for H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that solo-LTRs lack these marks.

claim: IAP elements were an exception, as their solo-LTRs were enriched for H3K9me3 on their own.
source: IAP elements were an exception, as their solo-LTRs were enriched for H3K9me3 on their own.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: H3K9me3 levels were rapidly modified between D0 and D6, while H3K27m3 gain lagged behind, reaching its full extent between D6 and D15.
source: Remarkably, different kinetics were observed for H3K9me3- and H3K27me3-related changes: H3K9me3 levels were rapidly modified between D0 and D6, while H3K27m3 gain lagged behind, reaching its full extent between D6 and D15.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Transposon families exhibited three general trends in 2i+vitC: A) co-occupancy of H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 (LINEs, MMERGLN, RLTR6, RLTR10, IAPEy, VL30), B) exclusive H3K9me3 occupation (IAPEz, MMERVK10C), and C) complete switch from H3K9me2/3 to H3K27me3-regulated chromatin (MERVL and MURVY).
source: From a universal H3K9me3 occupancy in serum, transposon families exhibited three general trends in 2i+vitC: A) co-occupancy of H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 (LINEs, MMERGLN, RLTR6, RLTR10, IAPEy, VL30), B) exclusive H3K9me3 occupation (IAPEz, MMERVK10C), and C) complete switch from H3K9me2/3 to H3K27me3-regulated chromatin (MERVL and MURVY) (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: IAPEz elements (category B) collectively gained H3K9me3 from D0 to D6.
source: IAPEz elements (category B) collectively gained H3K9me3 from D0 to D6; the MERVL and the Y-specific MURVY families (category C) also showed compact patterns, with individual elements transitioning together from H3K9me3 enrichment at D0 to H3K27me3 at D15 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The MERVL and the Y-specific MURVY families (category C) showed compact patterns, with individual elements transitioning together from H3K9me3 enrichment at D0 to H3K27me3 at D15.
source: IAPEz elements (category B) collectively gained H3K9me3 from D0 to D6; the MERVL and the Y-specific MURVY families (category C) also showed compact patterns, with individual elements transitioning together from H3K9me3 enrichment at D0 to H3K27me3 at D15 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Within the MMERGLN, RLTR6 or RLTR10 families, all elements gained H3K27me3 while maintaining or gaining high levels of H3K9me3.
source: Within the MMERGLN, RLTR6 or RLTR10 families, all elements gained H3K27me3 while maintaining or gaining high levels of H3K9me3.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Within the L1-T and IAPEy families, the majority of elements gained H3K27me3, but a subset maintained H3K9me3 without acquiring H3K27me3.
source: Within the L1-T and IAPEy families, the majority of elements gained H3K27me3, but a subset maintained H3K9me3 without acquiring H3K27me3 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K27me3 enrichment in RLTR4 was restricted to a small proportion of elements.
source: Another case of intra-familial heterogeneity is provided by RLTR4, which specifically carries H3K27me3 marks at D0 in serum: we demonstrate here that this enrichment was restricted to a small proportion of elements, as was previously suspected (Reichmann et al., 2012 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and a citation to Reichmann et al., 2012.

claim: H3K9me3 domains often spread out on adjacent genomic regions, whereas H3K27me3 was confined to transposon sequences.
source: Notably, H3K9me3 domains often spread out on adjacent genomic regions, whereas H3K27me3 was confined to transposon sequences (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq metaplot data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: H3K9me3 enrichment is restricted to the 5' UTR of LINEs.
source: It was previously described that H3K9me3 enrichment is restricted to the 5' UTR of LINEs, while being evenly distributed along the entire length of ERVs (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014; Pezic et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014 and Pezic et al., 2014.

claim: H3K9me3 is evenly distributed along the entire length of specific ERVK elements only, namely IAPEz, IAPEy and MMERKV10C.
source: In fact, we found this to be valid for specific ERVK elements only, namely IAPEz, IAPEy and MMERKV10C.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq metaplot data analysis.

claim: A spatial separation between H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 was observed in category A transposons: H3K9me3 tended to occupy the 5' end, while H3K27me3 preferentially targeted the 3' end.
source: Our most striking finding was the observation of a spatial separation between the two marks in category A transposons: H3K9me3 tended to occupy the 5' end, while H3K27me3 preferentially targeted the 3' end. This was observed for a significant proportion of LINEs and for several ERVs of the 1 or K classes (MMERGLN, RLTR6, MuRRS, RLTR10) (Figure 5C for visual examples).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Some category A families showed H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 co-localization in their 5' region (VL30, IAPEy, ETnERV).
source: However, some category A families showed H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 co-localization in their 5' region (VL30, IAPEy, ETnERV).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq metaplot data analysis.

claim: Analysis of available ChIP-seq datasets showed concordant H3K27me3 patterns between serum-grown Dnmt-tKO ES cells and 2i+vitC-grown ES cells.
source: Having demonstrated that culture-induced DNA demethylation leads to increased and family-specific distribution of H3K27me3 on transposon sequences, we reasoned that similar features might occur upon genetically induced DNA demethylation. Fulfilling this prediction, analysis of available ChIP-seq datasets (Brinkman et al., 2012) showed concordant H3K27me3 patterns between serum-grown Dnmt-tKO ES cells and 2i+vitC-grown ES cells: entire coverage of MERVL sequences, 3' localization in MMERGLN and RLTR6, and 5' localization in VL30 and ETnERV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and a citation to Brinkman et al., 2012.

claim: The pattern of H3K27me3 distribution on transposon sequences corresponds to an adaptation to the lack of DNA methylation.
source: These results support the notion that the pattern of H3K27me3 distribution on transposon sequences corresponds to an adaptation to the lack of DNA methylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the concordance between culture-induced and genetically-induced demethylation.

claim: Upon 2i+vitC-induced DNA demethylation, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 can converge on category A transposon sequences, but they occupy different territories.
source: In summary, upon 2i+vitC-induced DNA demethylation, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 can converge on category A transposon sequences, but they occupy different territories.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: IAPEz (category B) and MERVL (C) represent extreme cases of exclusivity, with the former being entirely covered by H3K9me3, and the latter by H3K27me3.
source: IAPEz (category B) and MERVL (C) represent extreme cases of exclusivity, with the former being entirely covered by H3K9me3, and the latter by H3K27me3.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: H3K27me3 deposition at transposons is a default response to the absence of both DNA and H3K9 methylation.
source: Our study provides unprecedented evidence that H3K27me3 deposition at transposons is a default response to the absence of both DNA and H3K9 methylation.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the chromatin data.

claim: L1 repression in serum relies on SUV39H-dependent H3K9me3 for L1-A, and very modestly for L1-T elements.
source: Previous studies concluded that L1 repression in serum relies on SUV39H-dependent H3K9me3 (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014): through the analysis of our genetic mutants, we found this was the case for L1-A, and very modestly for L1-T elements (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data in Suv39h-dKO cells shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, and a citation to Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014.

claim: LINE1 expression was significantly upregulated at the end of the conversion of Setdb1 +/- ES cells, suggesting an important role for SETDB1-mediated repression upon DNA methylation loss.
source: Moreover, LINE1 expression was significantly upregulated at the end of the conversion of Setdb1 +/- ES cells, suggesting an important role for SETDB1-mediated repression upon DNA methylation loss.
evidence: This is based on Nanostring data in Setdb1 +/- cells.

claim: Absence of polycomb had little effect on transposons in ES cells with a methylated genome (at D0 of conversion).
source: In regards to the role of polycomb, RNA-seq analysis of Eed-KO ES cells revealed that absence of polycomb had little effect on transposons in ES cells with a methylated genome (at D0 of conversion).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data in Eed-KO cells.

claim: Many transposon families, including the different young LINE1 subtypes that belong to the A category, were strongly activated in fully 2i+vitC-converted Eed-KO cells.
source: In contrast, many transposon families, including the different young LINE1 subtypes that belong to the A category, were strongly activated in fully 2i+vitC-converted Eed-KO cells (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1): polycomb-mediated silencing is therefore involved in controlling these transposons, specifically in absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Eed-KO cells shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Polycomb-mediated silencing is involved in controlling LINE1 transposons, specifically in absence of DNA methylation.
source: In contrast, many transposon families, including the different young LINE1 subtypes that belong to the A category, were strongly activated in fully 2i+vitC-converted Eed-KO cells (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1): polycomb-mediated silencing is therefore involved in controlling these transposons, specifically in absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data in Eed-KO cells.

claim: ERV families that gain H3K27me3 uniquely in their 3' end – such as MMERGLN, RLTR6 or RLTR10 – were not misregulated in absence of EED.
source: Interestingly, ERV families that gain H3K27me3 uniquely in their 3' end – such as MMERGLN, RLTR6 or RLTR10 – were not misregulated in absence of EED; this suggests that 3' end deposition of H3K27me3 does not drive their transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data in Eed-KO cells.

claim: 3' end deposition of H3K27me3 does not drive transcriptional repression of MMERGLN, RLTR6 or RLTR10.
source: Interestingly, ERV families that gain H3K27me3 uniquely in their 3' end – such as MMERGLN, RLTR6 or RLTR10 – were not misregulated in absence of EED; this suggests that 3' end deposition of H3K27me3 does not drive their transcriptional repression.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of misregulation in Eed-KO cells.

claim: During conversion, Trim28+/- and Setdb1+/- cells showed enhanced IAPEz up-regulation and repression failure after D6, in line with a major role of SETDB1-related H3K9me3 for controlling these elements in ES cells.
source: During conversion, Trim28+/- and Setdb1+/- cells showed enhanced IAPEz up-regulation and repression failure after D6, in line with a major role of SETDB1-related H3K9me3 for controlling these elements in ES cells (Matsui et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data in Trim28+/- and Setdb1+/- cells and a citation to Matsui et al., 2010.

claim: SUV39H depletion led to an unexpected IAPEz suppression upon conversion.
source: However, SUV39H depletion led to an unexpected IAPEz suppression upon conversion.
evidence: This is based on Nanostring data in Suv39h-dKO cells.

claim: Suv39h-dKO cells have acquired long-term compensatory mechanisms that prevent transient IAPEz activation upon DNA methylation loss.
source: One possible explanation is that Suv39h-dKO cells have acquired long-term compensatory mechanisms that prevent transient IAPEz activation upon DNA methylation loss.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain the unexpected observation.

claim: IAPEz elements were more strongly expressed in Eed-KO compared to WT cells during conversion.
source: Moreover, IAPEz elements were more strongly expressed in Eed-KO compared to WT cells during conversion (Figures 6B and Figure 7A,B), which is at odds with their apparent lack of H3K27me3 enrichment in ChIP-seq data (Figures 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring and RNA-seq data shown in Figures 6B and Figure 7A,B.

claim: IAPEz activation in Eed-KO cells did not emanate from a few discrete elements but represented a general trend.
source: Analysis of individual elements showed that this activation did not emanate from a few discrete elements but represented a general trend (Figures 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 7C.

claim: MERVL elements are primarily repressed by EHMT1/EHMT2-dependent H3K9me2 marks in serum.
source: MERVL elements are known to be primarily repressed by EHMT1/EHMT2-dependent H3K9me2 marks in serum (Maksakova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maksakova et al., 2013.

claim: MERVL silencing also strongly relied on SUV39H-control in serum.
source: We found that MERVL silencing also strongly relied on SUV39H-control in serum (Figure 6C), which correlates with a modest H3K9me3 enrichment in our ChIP-seq data.
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data in Suv39h-dKO cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SUV39H-dependent H3K9me3 became dispensable for MERVL silencing upon 2i+vitC conversion.
source: SUV39H-dependent H3K9me3 became dispensable for MERVL silencing upon 2i+vitC conversion, and the switch towards H3K27me3 control was perfectly correlated with a 15-fold expression increase in Eed-KO cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MERVL was the most highly activated transposon in absence of EED, as a result of a collective upregulation of all individual elements.
source: RNA-seq analysis indicates that MERVL was actually the most highly activated transposon in absence of EED, as a result of a collective upregulation of all individual elements (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: MERVL represents a striking model of epigenetic switch from H3K9 to H3K27 methylation-based repression, which occurs subsequently to DNA methylation loss.
source: MERVL therefore represents a striking model of epigenetic switch from H3K9 to H3K27 methylation-based repression, which occurs subsequently to DNA methylation loss.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the genetic and chromatin data.

claim: Polycomb-dependent control can be implemented in absence of SUV39H, even in cells with high DNA methylation levels.
source: Interestingly, we found that polycomb-dependent control can be implemented in absence of SUV39H, even in cells with high DNA methylation levels: while MERVL elements were upregulated by five-fold in Suv39h-dKO cells in serum grown-conditions, additional depletion of EED in Suv39-Eed-tKO cells led to a 20 fold increase compared to WT cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Nanostring data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MERVL silencing relies on histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: Finally, MERVL silencing was previously shown to rely on other histone modifiers, such as histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Macfarlan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Macfarlan et al., 2011.

claim: Treatment with the HDAC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) resulted in strong upregulation of MERVL in both serum and 2i+vitC conditions.
source: Treatment with the HDAC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) resulted in strong upregulation of MERVL in both serum and 2i+vitC conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that histone deacetylation is required for efficient silencing of MERVL, in presence or absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Histone deacetylation is required for efficient silencing of MERVL, in presence or absence of DNA methylation.
source: Treatment with the HDAC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) resulted in strong upregulation of MERVL in both serum and 2i+vitC conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that histone deacetylation is required for efficient silencing of MERVL, in presence or absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the TSA treatment data.

claim: Various transposon families residing in the mouse genome adopted a common regulatory fate: after an initial transcriptional burst, repression was re-established in a DNA methylation-independent manner.
source: Despite their heterogeneous origins and structures, we found that various transposon families residing in the mouse genome adopted a common regulatory fate: after an initial transcriptional burst, repression was re-established in a DNA methylation-independent manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Distinct combinations of H3K9me2/3 and H3K27m3 were observed among transposon families, defining three functional categories of chromatin-based responses to DNA methylation loss: joint H3K9me3 and H3K27m3 (A), H3K9me3-exclusive (B), and H3K27me3-exclusive (C).
source: Distinct combinations of H3K9me2/3 and H3K27me3 were observed among transposon families, defining three functional categories of chromatin-based responses to DNA methylation loss: joint H3K9me3 and H3K27m3 (A), H3K9me3-exclusive (B), and H3K27me3-exclusive (C) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Dnmt-tKO cells, which have endured long-term adaptation to a DNA methylation-free state, displayed similar transposon-specific chromatin patterns when grown in serum.
source: Importantly, Dnmt-tKO cells, which have endured long-term adaptation to a DNA methylation-free state, displayed similar transposon-specific chromatin patterns when grown in serum, which excludes a medium-related effect.
evidence: This is based on comparison of chromatin patterns between 2i+vitC and Dnmt-tKO cells.

claim: Various histone-based repression strategies are implemented upon DNA methylation loss, thereby safeguarding pluripotent cells against a multitude of heterogeneous transposon entities.
source: In conclusion, our work revises the previous assumption that DNA methylation is dispensable for transposon silencing in ES cells; rather, we reveal here that various histone-based repression strategies are implemented upon DNA methylation loss, thereby safeguarding pluripotent cells against a multitude of heterogeneous transposon entities.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: Repressive chromatin reorganization has been cytologically observed in primordial germ cells (PGCs) undergoing genome-wide demethylation.
source: Interestingly, repressive chromatin reorganization has also been cytologically observed in primordial germ cells (PGCs) undergoing genome-wide demethylation (Hajkova et al., 2008; Seki et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hajkova et al., 2008 and Seki et al., 2007.

claim: The relocalization of H3K27me3 at transposons and its co-occurrence with H3K9me3 was reported in hypomethylated PGCs.
source: Moreover, the relocalization of H3K27me3 at transposons and its co-occurrence with H3K9me3 was also reported in hypomethylated PGCs (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: The cellular system of serum to 2i+vitC conversion could represent an adequate model to study in vivo events of chromatin reprogramming occurring at transposons upon DNA methylation loss.
source: Our cellular system could therefore represent an adequate model to study in vivo events of chromatin reprogramming occurring at transposons upon DNA methylation loss.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the similarity to PGC observations.

claim: DNA methylation does not exert significant control over H3K9me3-targeting of transposons in ES cells.
source: The persistence of H3K9me3 upon loss of DNA methylation highlights that DNA methylation does not exert significant control over H3K9me3-targeting of transposons in ES cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H3K9me3 remains stable upon demethylation.

claim: Regions of persistent DNA methylation (RMRs) coincide with high H3K9me3 enrichment on transposon sequences in fully 2i+vitC-converted cells.
source: Interestingly, we consistently observed that regions of persistent DNA methylation (RMRs) coincide with high H3K9me3 enrichment on transposon sequences in fully 2i+vitC-converted cells, e.g. on the 5' end of LINE1 elements and throughout the length of ERVK elements.
evidence: This is based on comparison of WGBS and ChIP-seq data.

claim: H3K9me3 can confer protection against DNA demethylation.
source: This supports previous evidence that H3K9me3 can confer protection against DNA demethylation (Leung et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leung et al., 2014.

claim: The rapid disappearance of H3K9me2 upon serum to 2i+vitC conversion could reflect a direct role of DNA methylation in the maintenance of these marks.
source: Inversely, the rapid disappearance of H3K9me2 upon serum to 2i+vitC conversion could reflect a direct role of DNA methylation in the maintenance of these marks.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed correlation.

claim: H3K9me2 reduction was observed in DNA methylation-free Dnmt-tKO ES cells grown in serum.
source: Accordingly, H3K9me2 reduction was also observed in DNA methylation-free Dnmt-tKO ES cells grown in serum (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data.

claim: Coupled losses of DNA methylation and H3K9me2 have been previously reported in vivo, during normal primordial germ cell development and in DNA methylation-deficient spermatocytes.
source: Coupled losses of DNA methylation and H3K9me2 have also been previously reported in vivo, during normal primordial germ cell development (Hajkova et al., 2008; Seki et al., 2005) and in DNA methylation-deficient spermatocytes (Zamudio et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hajkova et al., 2008, Seki et al., 2005, and Zamudio et al., 2015.

claim: A mechanism of H3K9me2 methyltransferase recruitment via DNA methylation has been resolved in plants.
source: A mechanism of H3K9me2 methyltransferase recruitment via DNA methylation has been resolved in plants (Du et al., 2015); the evolution of an analogous mechanism in mammals should be explored.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Du et al., 2015.

claim: H3K27me3 is barely detectable at transposons in DNA hypermethylated WT ES cells grown in serum.
source: H3K27me3 is barely detectable at transposons in DNA hypermethylated WT ES cells grown in serum; in contrast, transposons accumulate H3K27me3 in both 2i+vitC-converted cells and in serum-grown Dnmt-tKO cells.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Transposons accumulate H3K27me3 in both 2i+vitC-converted cells and in serum-grown Dnmt-tKO cells.
source: H3K27me3 is barely detectable at transposons in DNA hypermethylated WT ES cells grown in serum; in contrast, transposons accumulate H3K27me3 in both 2i+vitC-converted cells and in serum-grown Dnmt-tKO cells.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: DNA methylation and H3K27me3 are mutually exclusive genome-wide and DNA methylation antagonizes H3K27me3 deposition.
source: This is in line with the prevailing notion that DNA methylation and H3K27me3 are mutually exclusive genome-wide and that DNA methylation antagonizes H3K27me3 deposition (Brinkman et al., 2012; Jermann et al., 2014; Tanay et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brinkman et al., 2012, Jermann et al., 2014, and Tanay et al., 2007.

claim: Polycomb is typically targeted to unmethylated GC-rich gene promoters in mammalian genomes.
source: In mammalian genomes, polycomb is typically targeted to unmethylated GC-rich gene promoters (Jermann et al., 2014; Mendenhall et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jermann et al., 2014 and Mendenhall et al., 2010.

claim: Transposon sequences have a GC content superior to the genome average.
source: Notably, transposon sequences have a GC content superior to the genome average (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B): this signature could be sufficient to attract polycomb-mediated H3K27me3 deposition in the absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The GC-rich signature of transposons could be sufficient to attract polycomb-mediated H3K27me3 deposition in the absence of DNA methylation.
source: Notably, transposon sequences have a GC content superior to the genome average (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B): this signature could be sufficient to attract polycomb-mediated H3K27me3 deposition in the absence of DNA methylation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the GC content observation.

claim: The BEND3 protein was identified as a sensor of DNA methylation states at pericentromeric repeats, recruiting polycomb-dependent H3K27me3 marks in Dnmt-tKO ES cells.
source: Intermediate methyl-sensitive DNA binding proteins may be involved: the BEND3 protein was recently identified as a sensor of DNA methylation states at pericentromeric repeats, recruiting polycomb-dependent H3K27me3 marks in Dnmt-tKO ES cells (Saksouk et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saksouk et al., 2014.

claim: H3K27me3 relocalization towards pericentromeric repeats was observed in hypomethylated 2i+vitC ES cells.
source: Interestingly, we also observed H3K27me3 relocalization towards pericentromeric repeats in hypomethylated 2i+vitC ES cells.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: The H3K36 demethylase KDM2B, which targets unmethylated CpG-rich sequences, was shown to recruit PRC1, potentially leading to H3K27me3 deposition through PRC2 recruitment.
source: Similarly, the H3K36 demethylase KDM2B, which targets unmethylated CpG-rich sequences, was shown to recruit PRC1, potentially leading to H3K27me3 deposition through PRC2 recruitment (Blackledge et al., 2014; Farcas et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blackledge et al., 2014 and Farcas et al., 2012.

claim: Comparable mechanisms involving BEND3, KDM2B and/or other methyl-sensitive DNA binding proteins might be at play for the recruitment of H3K27me3 at hypomethylated transposons.
source: Comparable mechanisms might be at play for the recruitment of H3K27me3 at hypomethylated transposons, involving BEND3, KDM2B and/or other methyl-sensitive DNA binding proteins.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known mechanisms.

claim: H3K27me3 invades the transposon space left unmarked by DNA methylation upon 2i+VitC conversion.
source: Thus, based on previous observations, we posit that H3K27me3 invades the transposon space left unmarked by DNA methylation upon 2i+VitC conversion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the study findings.

claim: The three possible chromatin configurations that the different transposon families adopt are determined by H3K9me3 occupancy.
source: Moreover, we provide evidence that the three possible chromatin configurations that the different transposon families adopt are further determined by H3K9me3 occupancy (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is inferred from the chromatin data and illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: Mutual exclusion between H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 marks has been previously documented at gene promoters and pericentromeric repeats.
source: Mutual exclusion between H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 marks has been previously documented at gene promoters and pericentromeric repeats (Mikkelsen et al., 2007; Peters et al., 2003), but not at transposons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mikkelsen et al., 2007 and Peters et al., 2003.

claim: Category B transposons, which constantly maintain H3K9me3 marks throughout their entire length, do not acquire H3K27me3-based chromatin even though they lose DNA methylation.
source: We found that category B transposons, which constantly maintain H3K9me3 marks throughout their entire length, do not acquire H3K27me3-based chromatin even though they lose DNA methylation.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: Category C transposons, exemplified by MERVL elements, become strongly enriched for H3K27me3 as H3K9me2/3 depletes during medium conversion.
source: In contrast, category C transposons, exemplified by MERVL elements, become strongly enriched for H3K27me3 as H3K9me2/3 depletes during medium conversion.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: As H3K9me3 constitutively marks the 5' end of category A transposons, only their 3' end is accessible to H3K27me3 deposition upon DNA methylation loss.
